hints: Count the total electrons for Co with atomic number 27, remembering the $1s^22s^22p^6$ core already accounts for 10 electrons, so 17 remain to place in 3s, 3p, 4s and 3d.
Recall the rule for forming a $2+$ transition metal ion, think about which subshell loses electrons first.
walkthrough:
Build the Co atom from atomic number 27**
You have 27 electrons to place. The first 10 are given as $1s^22s^22p^6$. The next 8 fill $3s^2 3p^6$ like argon, leaving 9 electrons. These go as $4s^2$ then $3d^7$, giving $1s^22s^22p^6 3s^23p^63d^74s^2$. Think of 4s filling before 3d when building the atom.

Remove electrons to make $Co^{2+}$**
When a transition metal forms a positive ion, electrons are always removed from 4s before 3d, even though 4s filled first. So remove the two $4s^2$ electrons completely. That leaves $1s^22s^22p^6 3s^23p^63d^7$ with no 4s electrons.

hints: Picture the structure, a central metal species with surrounding molecules or ions attached by dative bonds, and recall what the ligands must be called in the definition.
walkthrough:
Picture what a complex looks like**
Imagine $Co^{2+}$ in the middle with lone pairs from $Cl^-$ or $H_2O$ donating into its empty orbitals. That central metal plus its attached donors is the unit. So a complex ion is simply a central metal atom or ion surrounded by and bonded to ligands.
Final answer: A central metal atom or ion surrounded by / bonded to one or more ligands.

hints: Add up the charges, one $Co^{2+}$ plus four $Cl^-$ ligands, to work out the overall charge on the bracket.
Recall how to show tetrahedral 3D shape on paper, with two bonds in the plane, one solid wedge coming out and one hashed wedge going back.
walkthrough:
Work out the overall charge**
Add the parts: $+2$ from cobalt plus $4 \times (-1) = -4$ from chloride gives $-2$ overall. So the formula is $[CoCl_4]^{2-}$. Always show that $2-$ outside the drawing or bracket.

Draw tetrahedral in 3D**
Place Co in the centre with four $Co-Cl$ bonds arranged tetrahedrally, about $109.5^{\circ}$ apart. Draw two bonds as straight lines in the plane, one as a solid wedge coming towards you and one as a hashed wedge going away. Label each outer atom Cl.

Final answer: $[CoCl_4]^{2-}$, charge is $2-$
Tetrahedral drawing with Co at centre bonded to four Cl, using one solid wedge bond, one hashed wedge bond and two normal bonds, with $2-$ charge shown.

hints: Start from the isolated metal ion where all five d-orbitals have the same energy, then think what ligands do to split them into two sets.
Link the energy gap between the split d-orbitals to visible light, considering what happens when a photon of exactly that energy meets the complex.
Think about what happens to a single d-electron when it absorbs that photon and how the colour you see relates to the colours absorbed.
walkthrough:
Split the d-orbitals with ligands**
On its own, $Co^{2+}$ has five d-orbitals all at the same energy. When ligands approach, their lone pairs repel d-electrons unequally depending on orientation. This splits the set into two groups, a lower energy set and a higher energy set with a small gap that matches visible light energy.

Absorb light to jump the gap**
White light shines on the solution. A photon whose energy exactly equals the gap, $$\Delta E = h\nu$$, can be absorbed. That energy is used to promote an electron from a lower d-orbital to a vacant higher d-orbital. This is a d-d transition.

See the colour that is left**
The wavelengths absorbed are removed from white light. Your eye detects all the remaining wavelengths that pass through or are reflected. That mixture is the colour you observe, for example blue if red, orange and yellow are absorbed.

Final answer: Ligands cause the d-orbitals to split into two groups of different energy.
Visible light is absorbed to provide energy for d-d transition.
An electron is promoted / excited from a lower d-orbital to a higher d-orbital, the remaining transmitted light gives the observed colour.

hints: Remember the observed colour is the light not absorbed, so for a blue solution think about which region of the spectrum must pass through unchanged.
walkthrough:
Flip absorption to observation**
If the complex looks blue, that blue light must be reaching your eyes. That means photons in the blue region do not have the right energy for the d-d gap and are not absorbed, while photons of the complementary colours, red, orange, yellow and green, are absorbed to excite electrons.
Final answer: Blue light is not absorbed / red, yellow, orange and green light is absorbed, so blue is transmitted.

hints: Recall the familiar test with cobalt(II) chloride paper, think about the colour of anhydrous versus hydrated cobalt(II).
Identify what water does to the $Cl^-$ ligands around cobalt, consider the name for swapping one ligand for another.
walkthrough:
Recall the blue to pink change**
Blue crystals contain the tetrahedral $[CoCl_4]^{2-}$ ion. Adding water replaces $Cl^-$ ligands with $H_2O$ to give the octahedral pink $[Co(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$ ion. So you see blue going pink.

Name the ligand swap**
No change in oxidation state occurs, cobalt stays as +2. Only the ligands around it change, $Cl^-$ out and $H_2O$ in. That is ligand exchange, also called ligand substitution.

Final answer: colour change: blue to pink
type of reaction: ligand exchange / ligand substitution

hints: For $Co^{2+}$ to be oxidised, the other half-cell must have a more positive $E^{\ominus}$ than $E^{\ominus}(Co^{3+}/Co^{2+}) = +1.82$ V, so look for a very strong oxidant in the Data Booklet.
walkthrough:
Choose an oxidant stronger than $Co^{3+}$**
$E^{\ominus}$ for $Co^{3+} + e^- \rightleftharpoons Co^{2+}$ is very positive, $+1.82$ V, so $Co^{2+}$ is hard to oxidise. You need an oxidising agent with an even more positive $E^{\ominus}$. From the Data Booklet, $F_2/F^-$ at $+2.87$ V and $S_2O_8^{2-}/SO_4^{2-}$ at $+2.01$ V both qualify.
Final answer: $F_2$ or $S_2O_8^{2-}$

hints: Use $$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{cathode} - E^{\ominus}_{anode}$$ with the oxidant as cathode and $+1.82$ V for the cobalt couple as anode.
walkthrough:
Subtract to get $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$**
Take the more positive oxidant couple minus the cobalt couple. For fluorine: $$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = +2.87 - (+1.82) = +1.05\,\text{V}$$ For peroxodisulfate: $$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = +2.01 - (+1.82) = +0.19\,\text{V}$$ A positive value confirms the reaction is feasible.
Final answer: $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = +1.05$ V (using $F_2$) or $+0.19$ V (using $S_2O_8^{2-}$)

hints: Combine $Co^{2+} \rightarrow Co^{3+} + e^-$ with the reduction of your chosen oxidant, balancing electrons to give the overall ionic equation.
walkthrough:
Balance the redox pair**
Oxidation is $Co^{2+} \rightarrow Co^{3+} + e^-$. Reduction for fluorine is $F_2 + 2e^- \rightarrow 2F^-$. Multiply the cobalt half-equation by 2 to balance electrons, then add: $$2Co^{2+} + F_2 \rightarrow 2Co^{3+} + 2F^-$$ The peroxodisulfate version balances similarly: $$2Co^{2+} + S_2O_8^{2-} \rightarrow 2Co^{3+} + 2SO_4^{2-}$$
Final answer: $2Co^{2+} + F_2 \rightarrow 2Co^{3+} + 2F^-$ or $2Co^{2+} + S_2O_8^{2-} \rightarrow 2Co^{3+} + 2SO_4^{2-}$

hints: In an octahedral $[Co(NH_3)_3(NO_2)_3]$ complex, think about how three identical ligands can be arranged, either all on one face or around the middle.
For the trans or fac-mer distinction used here, consider the $N-Co-N$ bond angles, when two $NO_2^-$ groups are opposite each other one angle is $180^{\circ}$.
Recall the general name for this type of spatial difference in octahedral complexes with monodentate ligands.
walkthrough:
Draw the trans (mer) isomer**
Put Co at the centre of an octahedron. Place the three $NO_2^-$ ligands so two are opposite each other, giving one $180^{\circ}$ $N-Co-N$ angle and two $90^{\circ}$ angles. The three $NH_3$ ligands fill the remaining three sites in the same meridian plane. Show wedges for 3D depth.

Draw the cis (fac) isomer**
Now cluster all three $NO_2^-$ ligands on one triangular face of the octahedron, so every $N-Co-N$ angle is $90^{\circ}$ with no opposite pair. The three $NH_3$ ligands occupy the opposite face. This is the facial arrangement.

Name the isomerism**
Both have the same formula $[Co(NH_3)_3(NO_2)_3]$ but different spatial positions of monodentate ligands around the octahedron. That is cis-trans isomerism, also called geometric isomerism.

Final answer: Isomer 1 (trans / mer): two $O_2N-Co-NO_2$ angles $90^{\circ}$, one $180^{\circ}$, three $NH_3$ also mer arrangement.
Isomer 2 (cis / fac): all three $O_2N-Co-NO_2$ angles $90^{\circ}$, all three ligands occupy one face of octahedron.
type of isomerism: cis-trans / geometric
